failures.title: BMW N73B60 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: VANOS Seal Degradation - Loss of Low-End Power & Rough Idle
items.whatHappens: The N73's VANOS system (double VANOS) relies on rubber seals that degrade over time, allowing oil pressure to bleed past the seals. This causes poor low-end power, rough idle, hesitation on acceleration, and increased fuel consumption. This is the single most common issue on the N73, affecting virtually all examples as they age.
items.repairVsReplace: VANOS seal replacement is a specialist job (£1,500-£2,500) and requires removal of the cylinder heads. While labour-intensive, it's far cheaper than a full engine replacement. Many owners combine this with timing chain replacement and valve stem seal work while the heads are off. → Read our full VANOS failure guide

items.title: Ignition Coil Failure - Misfires on the V12
items.whatHappens: The N73's ignition coils are mounted under the intake manifold and are exposed to engine heat. They can fail, causing misfires, rough running, and check-engine lights. On a V12, coil failure on one cylinder is noticeable and can lead to limp mode.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil replacement is a straightforward job (£300-£600 for all 12 coils) but requires removing the intake manifold to access the coils. Many owners replace all 12 coils as a preventative measure when the intake manifold is off for other work. → Read our full ignition coil failure guide

items.title: Valve Stem Seal Wear - Oil Consumption & Blue Smoke
items.whatHappens: The N73's valve stem seals degrade over time, allowing oil to seep past them into the combustion chambers. This manifests as blue smoke on cold start-up and, in severe cases, during driving. This is particularly common on higher-mileage examples and those with long oil change intervals.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a labour-intensive job (£2,000-£4,000) and requires removal of the cylinder heads. If the engine is out for other work (e.g., VANOS overhaul), many owners combine this with the seal replacement. If the car is high-mileage and has other issues, a reconditioned unit may be more cost-effective.

failures.goodYearsLine: The N73 was revised in 2005 (LCI models) with updated engine management and minor hardware refinements. However, the VANOS seal and ignition coil issues affect all N73 engines regardless of production year - these are material degradation issues, not production-run problems.

variants.title: N73B60 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The N73B60 was produced in two main variants across the 7-Series generation: the N73B60A (pre-LCI) and the N73B60B (LCI). The differences are in engine management and minor hardware updates, not in the block or cylinder head design. - Fitted to: E65/E66 760i / 760Li (2003-2005), Rolls-Royce Phantom (some early models) - Key technical difference: 445 hp output, earlier DME (engine management) version, specific exhaust calibration, Euro 3/4 emissions compliance - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family VANOS seal and coil failure patterns; pre-LCI engines have more frequent VANOS issues due to earlier seal material - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the N73B60B - ECU, wiring and emissions systems differ. Requires full electronics transplant if swapping between generations - Fitted to: E65/E66 760i / 760Li (2005-2008), Rolls-Royce Phantom (2005-2008) - Key technical difference: 453 hp output, updated DME software, revised exhaust calibration for improved emissions, minor VANOS control refinements - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family VANOS seal and coil failure patterns; improved software but the physical seal degradation remains - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with earlier N73B60A - ECU, wiring and emissions architecture differ. Use the correct variant for your chassis - Fitted to: Rolls-Royce Phantom (2003-2008) - Key technical difference: Badged as 6.75L V12 (actual displacement 6.0L), specific Rolls-Royce ECU calibration for ultra-smooth power delivery, different intake/exhaust tuning - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family VANOS seal and coil failure patterns; Rolls-Royce models may have lower mileage but the same age-related seal degradation - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with BMW-spec engines - ECU calibration, ancillaries and cooling system differ. Use Rolls-Royce-spec engines for Phantom replacements

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement N73B60 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used N73B60 is a risky proposition unless it comes from a very low-mileage car with full documented history and proof of recent VANOS overhaul and coil replacement. The V12's complexity means many used engines have hidden issues (VANOS seals, coil failures, valve stem seal wear). Only consider a used unit with proof of recent work in these areas. Factor in £2,000-£4,000 for preventative work (VANOS seals, coils, valve stem seals) if the history is unclear. Link once: /services/used-engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper N73B60 recon is the only sensible choice for owners of high-value 7-Series V12s or Rolls-Royce Phantoms. A quality recon should include: full strip and inspection, new VANOS seals (critical), new ignition coils and injectors, new valve stem seals, new gaskets and seals, and a full test. With a 12-24 month warranty, this gives you a fresh engine with all known weaknesses engineered out - well worth the £6,000-£9,000 supply cost for a flagship BMW. Link once: /services/reconditioned-engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified when the original engine has suffered catastrophic failure (overheating, oil starvation) and the car is a cherished example (especially low-mileage E65 760i or Phantom). An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons/rings, refreshed cylinder heads, new timing chains and guides, and a full VANOS overhaul. This is specialist territory and typically only makes sense for cars with strong residual value (£15,000+). Link once: /services/rebuilt-engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted BMW V12 specialists nationwide, with 12-month warranty on reconditioned and rebuilt units. Link once: /services/supply-and-fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The N73B60 sits in E65/E66 760i - cars now worth £3,000-£15,000 depending on condition and mileage, and Rolls-Royce Phantom - cars worth £30,000-£80,000+. With a reconditioned supply cost of £6,000-£9,000, replacement is viable on higher-value 7-Series examples and easily justified on a Phantom. However, for a high-mileage 760i worth under £5,000, a used unit (£3,000-£5,000) may be the only sensible option - and even then, evaluate whether the car's overall condition justifies the spend. For cars worth under £4,000 with significant body or suspension wear, consider breaking the car before committing to a replacement engine.

items.answer: The most documented issues are VANOS seal degradation (causing loss of low‑end power and rough idle), ignition coil failure (misfires on the V12), and valve stem seal wear (causing oil consumption and blue smoke). These three issues are the N73 family's most notorious weaknesses, affecting all variants regardless of production year. → Read our full VANOS failure guide.
